outcomes.original: Filing step: Form the legal entity (LLC or corporation) with the California Secretary of State and obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS. What to say: File online at the Secretary of State's bizfile portal (LLC Articles of Organization, $70; corporation, $100) and apply for the EIN at irs.gov the same day. The EIN is issued immediately Monday–Friday. Both are prerequisites for the San Francisco business registration, the seller's permit, and the ABC license application. File the Statement of Information within 90 days of registering the entity ($20 for an LLC, due every two years; $25 for a corporation, due yearly).

outcomes.original: Filing step: Register the business with the San Francisco Office of the Treasurer & Tax Collector to obtain a Business Account Number (BAN). What to say: Register online within 30 days of starting business in San Francisco. The registration year runs April 1 to March 31; renewal is due by the last day of February. Fees are tiered by gross receipts: $55 up to $100k, $95 up to $250k, $625 at $1–1.5M for 2026–27, each plus a $4 state fee. Every other city department (Planning, DPH, DBI, ABC) requires the BAN, so obtain it before filing any permit application.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File a Fictitious Business Name (DBA) statement with the San Francisco County Clerk if the public-facing name differs from the legal entity name. What to say: File in person (bring photo ID) or by mail with the County Clerk. Publish the statement in a court-approved newspaper once a week for four weeks, then file proof of publication within 45 days. Total time 1–35 days, cost $60–$120. Banks and ABC require the filed statement, so complete this before opening the business bank account and applying for the ABC license.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File the Conditional Use Authorization application with San Francisco Planning for a change of use from limited restaurant to full-service restaurant with alcohol service. What to say: State that the concept is a bona fide eating place serving beer and wine (or full liquor, if that is the plan) incidental to meals, not a bar. Cite the September 2024 approval at 1457 Haight Street (Case No. 2024-004781CUA, Motion No. 21606) for the identical limited-to-full-service upgrade with no construction, and request the same standard conditions. Attach a menu, floor plan, and a good-neighbor policy. The application fee for a no-construction CUA is approximately $3,150 (2024–25 rate, CPI-adjusted yearly); new storefront businesses may qualify for a First Year Free fee waiver. Planning will route the application to DPH, Police, and other departments for review, schedule a Planning Commission hearing with 300-foot mailed notice and posted notice, and allow a 30-day appeal period after approval.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Apply for the ABC license (Type 41 for beer and wine, or Type 47 for full liquor) after the CUA is approved or during the CUA review if ABC will accept a contingent application. What to say: Submit the ABC application online with a copy of the signed lease, the seller's permit, the entity registration, the DBA statement, and the San Francisco business registration. For a Type 41 (beer and wine, eating place), the application takes 60–120 days and costs $1,000–$1,600; ABC will post a 30-day public notice at the premises and send the application to the Police Department ABC Liaison Unit and Planning for review. For a Type 47 (full liquor, eating place), you must first purchase an existing license on the open market ($100k–$450k in San Francisco) and file a person-to-person and premises-to-premises transfer, which takes 90–240 days. If the census tract is an undue-concentration tract, ABC will require a Public Convenience or Necessity (PCN) letter from the city, adding 1–3 months; start that process with the Police Department ABC Liaison Unit before filing the ABC application.
outcomes.note: The record shows only the undue-concentration flag; it does not state the license types, costs, timelines, procedures, or PCN requirements.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Obtain a California seller's permit from CDTFA and register as an employer with EDD if you have employees. What to say: Register online at the CDTFA portal for the seller's permit (free, often issued same day) and at the EDD e-Services for Business portal to register as an employer (free, 1–7 days). ABC will not issue a license until the seller's permit exists. Your payroll provider will need the EDD account number before the first pay run. Workers' compensation insurance is mandatory from the first employee; quote through a broker or the State Compensation Insurance Fund.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Apply for the health permit to operate at least one month before opening, after a certified food safety manager is on staff. What to say: Apply online with the BAN, Location ID (LIN), and federal tax ID. The FY2026–27 permit-to-operate application fee is $470 (includes initial inspection); the annual license fee for restaurants and bars is $0 for 2026–28. DPH will schedule a final inspection; the permit is issued after the inspection confirms the facility matches the approved plans, surfaces are sealed, hand sinks are installed, hot water is available, and a certified food safety manager is on staff. A change of ownership or entity type requires a new permit. Do not serve the public before the permit is issued. If the space requires any remodel or new equipment, submit a health plan check first with scaled drawings, photos, a menu, and an equipment list; approval takes 21–60 days.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File the building permit application for change of use with DBI, after the CUA is approved. What to say: The building permit must conform to the Planning Code before it is issued, so file after the CUA is approved and the 30-day appeal period has passed. If no construction is proposed, the permit application is for change of use without tenant improvements. DBI will route the application to Planning for zoning review, and over-the-counter approval may be possible if the use is principally permitted under the CUA and no neighborhood notification is triggered. Fees are a percentage of construction valuation; for a no-work change of use, expect a base fee of $800–$1,500. The building permit must be issued before the health permit final inspection.
outcomes.note: The zoning district record contains only district identification and address matching information, not filing procedures, fees, or permit requirements.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 120 to 300 days. Estimated government cost: $3,100 to $15,000. Notes: These are the days and government fees to obtain the three approvals in the entitlement path (Conditional Use Authorization, health permit to operate, and building permit with change of use) when they are granted. The CUA is the critical path: 120–300 days from filing to Planning Commission approval, including pre-application consultation, environmental review, 300-foot mailed notice, posted notice, the hearing, and a 30-day appeal period. The health permit takes 14–45 days after the final inspection is passed. The building permit for change of use without construction is routed to Planning for zoning review and may be issued over-the-counter in 14–90 days once the CUA is approved. Government fees: approximately $3,100–$15,000 for the CUA (higher with construction cost; new businesses may qualify for First Year Free fee waiver), $470–$1,000 for the health permit, and $800–$15,000 for the building permit (higher with construction). The ABC license is not included because the licence type is not specified: a Type 41 adds 60–120 days and $1,000–$1,600; a Type 47 transfer adds 90–240 days and $17,000–$450,000 (mostly license purchase price). If the census tract is an undue-concentration tract, add 1–3 months for a PCN letter. These figures are for approvals, not denials or withdrawals.
